clue.text: Second husband beset by awful pain beginning to emerge healthy

indicators.note: to be beset by something is to be surrounded by it, so the pair of letters sits inside
awful suggests something badly made, so the letters of pain are jumbled

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband in family trees and lists

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, here the first of emerge

parts.note: the first letter of emerge

explanation.surface: A man laid low by terrible pain finally comes out of it in good health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' jumbles PAIN into INAP; 'beset by' puts S and H inside it; 'beginning to' adds the E of emerge.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in shape is an idiom for being physically fit and well.

clue.text: One mobilising about pit is type proposed for office

indicators.note: about means going round, so the jumbled letters are placed around the next piece
mobilising means setting in motion, so the letters of one are moved into a new order

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: Someone organising a protest around a coal pit turns out to be a candidate for election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mobilising' turns ONE into NOE, and 'about' puts it round MINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominee is a person put forward as a candidate for a position or office.

clue.text: Movable joint is put in something easily

indicators.note: the answer is lodged inside the following words

parts.note: the last four letters of 'something' plus the first of 'easily'

explanation.surface: A joint that can be moved is fitted into something without much effort.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles two words: somet[HING E]asily. 'Movable joint' sounds anatomical, but a door hinge fits just as well.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinge is a joint that lets a door or lid swing.

clue.text: Eccentric temping gets natural colouring matter

indicators.note: an eccentric version of TEMPING has its letters out of order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: An odd temporary worker acquires some natural colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' reads as describing a person doing temp work; here it only tells you to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigment is the substance that gives skin, plants or paint their colour.

clue.text: Classify businessman's first dishonest scheme

indicators.note: take only the opening letter of 'businessman'

parts.note: first letter of businessman
a racket is a dishonest scheme

explanation.surface: Someone labels a businessman's first shady scheme for what it is.
explanation.walkthrough: To bracket things is to group them together into a class.
explanation.definitionFit: To bracket items is to put them in the same category.

clue.text: Manage area in wide yard as feature of an airport

parts.note: to run a business is to manage it

indicators.note: in places the area letter inside the pair of letters for wide and yard

parts.note: W is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a wide

explanation.surface: Someone is told to manage a space in a broad yard as part of an airport.
explanation.walkthrough: A wide is a cricket delivery out of the batter's reach, scored as W.
explanation.definitionFit: A runway is the strip on which aircraft take off and land, a central part of any airport.

clue.text: Richard shortly entering Crete for recreation is one playing on a square

indicators.note: entering means going into, so the name sits inside the rearranged island
recreation read as re-creation means making again, so the letters of Crete are rebuilt

parts.note: Rick is a short form of the name Richard

explanation.surface: A man called Richard goes to Crete on holiday and turns out to be a sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' tells you to use the short form of Richard. 'for recreation' rearranges CRETE into CETER, which RICK enters. A square is the closely mown central area of a cricket field where the pitches are.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricketer plays on the square, the strip of the ground where cricket pitches are prepared.

clue.text: Improve education at the margins with opportunity initially missed

indicators.note: the margins of a word are its outside letters, its first and last

parts.note: the first and last letters of education

indicators.note: the first letter is missed, so it is dropped from the word for opportunity

parts.note: a chance is an opportunity

explanation.surface: A call to improve schooling that is marginal, with chances missed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the margins' takes EN from education; 'initially missed' drops the C of CHANCE to leave HANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance something is to make it better or increase its quality.

clue.text: Fancy reception's fit for one with impossibly high standards

indicators.note: a fancy version of the words is an elaborate rearrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: An elegant party is judged suitable for a guest who is never satisfied.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S is part of the fodder: it supplies the S the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: A perfectionist refuses to accept anything short of flawless.

clue.text: Sign of things to come found among some neighbours

indicators.note: the answer is located among the letters of the next words

parts.note: the tail of 'some' runs into the first letter of 'neighbours'

explanation.surface: A portent of the future turns up among the people next door.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the gap between two words: s[OME N]eighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a portent, good or bad, foretelling future events.

clue.text: Environmentalist of a delicate nature gets permission to go ahead?

parts.note: a Green is an environmental campaigner
light = delicate, as in a light touch

explanation.surface: A gentle environmental campaigner is finally given approval for a project.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is a figure of speech: a traffic signal standing for approval.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the green light means being allowed to proceed, like a traffic signal.

clue.text: A pair of notes by West Country banker in addition to a building

parts.note: used as it stands
n = note, twice
a banker is a river (it has banks); the Exe flows through Devon

explanation.surface: Two banknotes are handed over by a West Country bank manager on top of a building deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' is a crossword joke for a river. The West Country is south-west England, and the Exe runs through Exeter.
explanation.definitionFit: An annexe is an extra building or wing joined to a main one.

clue.text: Fellow following with no end of interest method of extracting gas

parts.note: f = fellow

parts.words: following with no end of interest
parts.note: TRACKING (following) minus T, the last letter of 'interest'

explanation.surface: A man trails along, bored, behind a new technique for getting gas out of the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The T removed is the end of 'interest', not of 'following'. Fracking forces fluid into rock to release gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Fracking cracks underground rock with pressurised fluid to extract gas.

clue.text: Manic set's manipulated shades of meaning

definitions.note: Semantics is a singular noun; the plural definition treats it as the nuances themselves.

indicators.note: the letters are handled and moved about

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A frantic group has twisted the finer points of what was said.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S counts as a letter of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Semantics is the meaning of words, including their fine distinctions.

clue.text: Random piece penned by a bishop on a railway

parts.note: used as it stands

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first part sits on top of what follows

parts.note: RR = Right Reverend, a bishop's title
a bit is a piece
used as it stands
ry = railway

explanation.surface: A stray fragment of writing turns up, composed by a bishop while travelling by train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned' looks like writing, but it means enclosed, as in a sheep pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Arbitrary means random, not based on reason.

clue.text: Hard material has support in confines of school

indicators.note: in places the support inside the outer letters of school
the confines of something are its edges, so the first and last letters of school

parts.note: the first and last letters of school
a tee is a peg that supports a golf ball

explanation.surface: Something tough props up the walls of a school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confines of' takes SL from school, and TEE goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Steel is an alloy of iron known for its strength and hardness.

clue.text: Mention of wealthy people making projections

indicators.note: to mention something is to say it, so the answer is how the word sounds

parts.note: nobs is British slang for posh, rich people; the word you hear has a silent K in front

explanation.surface: Talk of the rich turns to their investment forecasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nobs' is British slang for upper-class or wealthy people. 'Projections' looks like forecasts but means things that stick out.
explanation.definitionFit: Knobs are rounded lumps that project from a surface.

clue.text: Grey person with no allegiance to either side

definitions.meaning: an adjective for a muted colour with no strong hue

definitions.text: person with no allegiance to either side
definitions.meaning: a noun for a country or person staying out of a conflict

explanation.surface: An unremarkable fence-sitter who backs neither camp.
explanation.walkthrough: Grey is both a neutral shade and a description of a dull, uncommitted person, so the two halves blur.
explanation.definitionFit: Neutral names both a muted colour and someone who takes no side.

clue.text: Separate from friend left to wander overlooking lake

indicators.note: to wander is to stray from a set path, so the letters of friend and what remains of left are rearranged
overlooking means ignoring, so the lake letter is passed over and dropped from left

parts.note: L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Someone is cut off from a friend who has been left to roam beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' drops the L for lake from LEFT to leave EFT; 'to wander' then rearranges FRIEND with EFT.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are different are distinct from one another, as separate items are.

clue.text: One establishing an institution gets to be unsuccessful

definitions.meaning: a noun: the person who sets up a school, charity or firm
a verb: to fail, originally of a ship filling and sinking

explanation.surface: The person who set up an organisation ends up failing.
explanation.walkthrough: The noun and the verb are spelt the same but have unrelated roots.
explanation.definitionFit: A founder establishes something; to founder is to collapse or fail.

clue.text: Figure before ten has secure thing put in an alley?

parts.note: nine comes just before ten
to pin is to secure

explanation.surface: A number just short of ten comes with a way of fastening something.
explanation.walkthrough: The alley is a skittle alley, where ninepins are set up to be knocked down; the question mark hints at that.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: these skittles are stood at the end of a skittle alley to be bowled at.

clue.text: Twin has drink twice the normal measure

definitions.meaning: what you order at a bar for two measures of spirits

explanation.surface: One twin orders a large whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' works only as a joining word here, though the surface reads it as the twin having a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A double is both a person's twin-like lookalike and a two-measure drink.

clue.text: Finally catch leaders of heist unsettling new director in built-up area

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters, here of heist and unsettling

parts.note: the first letters of these two words

indicators.note: in places the director letter inside the word for a built-up area

parts.note: a town is a built-up area

explanation.surface: A robbery shakes up a new film director in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders of' gives HU, then N; 'in' puts D into TOWN to make TDOWN.
explanation.definitionFit: To hunt someone down is an idiom for tracking them until you catch them.

clue.text: Suave Republican graduate in a French café lately

indicators.note: the RBA goes inside the other letters

parts.note: un is French for a
r = Republican
BA = Bachelor of Arts

indicators.note: late in the word: its final letter

parts.note: last letter of café

explanation.surface: A smooth American politician holding a degree lounges in a Paris café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lately' does not mean recently here; it points to the late, or last, letter of 'café'.
explanation.definitionFit: Urbane means smoothly courteous and sophisticated, which is suave.

clue.text: Heavily built liberal in part of Greater Manchester

parts.note: Bury is a town in Greater Manchester, in north-west England
l = liberal

explanation.surface: A strapping Liberal politician is found in a corner of north-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: Greater Manchester is a metropolitan county made of ten boroughs, so any of its towns can be the 'part'.
explanation.definitionFit: Burly describes a large, strong, heavily built person.

clue.text: General journalist following Barbados in a storm

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the journalist goes after the scrambled island
something in a storm is tossed about, so the letters of Barbados are scrambled

parts.note: ED, short for editor, is the crossword journalist

explanation.surface: An army general reports on Barbados during a hurricane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like a military rank but is the adjective. 'in a storm' scrambles BARBADOS into BROADBAS, and 'following' puts ED after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad-based means drawing on a wide range of things, so wide-ranging or general in scope.

clue.text: Chewy meat with time gone is ready to eat

parts.note: tripe, cow's stomach lining, is famously chewy
t = time, removed

explanation.surface: Tough meat that has been left out a while is declared fit to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIPE loses its T to leave RIPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for fruit or cheese that has matured enough to be eaten.

clue.text: Favoured including unprofessional line in short drama

parts.note: a pet project is a favoured one
lay = not professional, as in a layman
l = line

explanation.surface: A favourite actor includes a clumsy amateur line in a brief play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Favoured' is an adjective here, as in a favoured child, which is why it can be a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: The -let ending means small, so the word names a brief play.

clue.text: Female with Gary in ground describing some old clothes?

indicators.note: ground here is the past of grind, so the letters of Gary and in are crushed into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman and a man called Gary are on the pitch, discussing worn garments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like a football pitch but is the past tense of grind: it rearranges GARY and IN into RAYING.
explanation.definitionFit: Old clothes that are fraying are coming apart at the seams and edges with wear.
